# Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

### Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a dominant global cardiovascular challenge associated with high morbidity, frequent hospitalizations, and premature mortality. Historically, pharmacological strategies focused primarily on neurohormonal blockade. However, the introduction of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) revolutionized this paradigm. Sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class ARNI, combines the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan. This dual mechanism enhances beneficial vasoactive peptides (such as natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin) while simultaneously blocking the deleterious effects of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) on angiotensin II type 1 ($AT_1$) receptors. Early proof-of-concept was established in Phase II trials, such as PARAMOUNT, which demonstrated significant reductions in natriuretic peptides in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [22].

### Clinical Efficacy in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
The therapeutic efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in chronic HFrEF was established by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. In this study of 8,399 patients, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite primary outcome of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% compared with enalapril [1]. Furthermore, the ARNI was shown to significantly reduce sudden cardiac death [24], slow clinical progression [20], and improve health-related quality of life [25] compared to standard angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) therapy. 

Subsequent studies focused on the initiation and optimization of ARNI therapy. The TITRATION trial outlined safe up-titration regimens [21], while the TRANSITION study showed that sacubitril/valsartan could be safely initiated in-hospital in stabilized patients following an acute decompensation event [6]. The PIONEER-HF trial expanded this evidence to acute decompensated HF, demonstrating that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and a lower risk of rehospitalization compared to enalapril [2]. 

Beyond clinical events, the mechanism of benefit has been linked to positive cardiac remodeling. The PROVE-HF trial showed a strong correlation between NT-proBNP reduction and improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) alongside decreases in left ventricular volumes [4]. Similarly, the EVALUATE-HF trial confirmed a reduction in aortic stiffness and a decline in left ventricular end-diastolic volume index over 12 weeks of therapy [5]. Given these robust findings, a patient-level meta-analysis estimated that transition from conventional therapy to a comprehensive regimen containing an ARNI translates into several years of additional life expectancy [12].

### Expanding the Ejection Fraction Spectrum (HFpEF and HFmrEF)
Extending these successes, the PARAGON-HF trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan against valsartan alone in patients with HFpEF (LVEF $\ge$45%) [3]. Although the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint, pre-specified subgroup analyses revealed a distinct clinical benefit in patients with an LVEF below normal (approximately 45%–57%) and in women [3,13,18]. To address acute stabilization in this cohort, the PARAGLIDE-HF trial enrolled patients with an LVEF >40% who had recently experienced a worsening HF event, finding a significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP with sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan [10]. Participant-level pooled analyses of PARAGON-HF and PARAGLIDE-HF consolidated the evidence, highlighting a reduction in cardiovascular and renal events across the spectrum of mildly reduced and lower preserved ejection fractions [11,13]. Conversely, in the post-myocardial infarction setting, the PARADISE-MI trial compared sacubitril/valsartan to ramipril in high-risk patients but did not show a statistically significant reduction in the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint [7].

### Special Populations, Safety, and Tolerability
The safety and tolerability of sacubitril/valsartan have been thoroughly characterized. In advanced HFrEF (NYHA Class IV), the LIFE trial showed that while sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly lower NT-proBNP compared to valsartan alone, it maintained a comparable safety profile, though with a higher rate of non-life-threatening hyperkalemia [8]. In pediatric populations, the PANORAMA-HF trial confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan is well tolerated and offers clinical efficacy comparable or superior to enalapril in pediatric patients with systemic ventricular systolic dysfunction [9]. 

Renal outcomes are critically tied to HF prognosis. Sacubitril/valsartan provides superior renal protection compared to traditional RAAS inhibitors. The UK HARP-III trial demonstrated comparable renal safety and blood pressure control in patients with chronic kidney disease [23]. Secondary analyses of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that ARNI therapy significantly slows the rate of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline [27,29] and reduces the risk of severe hyperkalemia, even in patients concomitantly treated with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) [26]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan is associated with improved glycemic control, reducing HbA1c levels in diabetic HF patients [17] and showing an expected profile of blood pressure lowering [19], thus demonstrating multi-organ benefits.

### Real-world Evidence and Current Guidelines
The clinical utility of sacubitril/valsartan is supported by extensive real-world evidence. Large registry data from the CHAMP-HF registry showed rapid and substantial improvements in patient-reported health status and symptom burdens shortly after initiating therapy [30]. Systematic reviews of real-world cohorts have consistently mirrored the efficacy and safety profile reported in randomized trials [28]. 

Reflecting this overwhelming body of evidence, both the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA [14] and the 2021 ESC [15] guidelines have designated ARNI as a Class I first-line recommendation for patients with chronic HFrEF. The guidelines also support its consideration in patients with heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) and selected patients with HFpEF, establishing sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational pillar of modern heart failure therapy.
